messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elijah Mensah, a distinguished 68-year-old policy analyst, had always prided himself on his sharp intellect and steady composure. That changed irrevocably a year ago when, while presenting a complex economic brief to a parliamentary committee, he felt a crushing weight in his chest. The next hours blurred into a terrifying kaleidoscope of flashing lights, frantic voices, and the searing pain of a heart attack. He remembered the metallic taste in his mouth, the feeling of his body shutting down, and the chilling thought that this was the end. Though he survived, undergoing emergency surgery and a prolonged recovery, the experience left an indelible mark, transforming his inner world.

Now, a year later, Elijah found himself a prisoner in his own skin. When he tried to recount the event, he could describe the sequence of medical procedures with remarkable accuracy, almost clinically, but he felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. This emotionless recall was a stark contrast to other moments when, without warning, a sudden beep from his kitchen timer or the sterile scent of cleaning fluid would plunge him back into the hospital room. In those moments, the memory felt like it was happening right now rather than something that was over; he would feel the phantom pressure in his chest, hear the urgent murmurs of the medical staff, and experience the terror as if it were fresh. When these intrusive memories returned, he felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes needing several minutes to regain his bearings, his breath catching in his throat.

His body, once a reliable vessel, had become an unpredictable adversary. He had come to believe, with a profound sense of betrayal, that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe. His muscles felt constantly tense and ready to react, his heart often racing for no apparent reason, a perpetual vigilance that left him exhausted. What frightened him most was the pervasive feeling that he could no longer trust his own body; every minor ache or flutter was interpreted as a harbinger of another catastrophic event. Even within the familiar walls of his own home, a place that had always been his sanctuary, he felt on guard, startled by the creaks of the old house or the sudden ring of his phone.

This constant internal turmoil had severely impacted his professional life. As a policy analyst, his work demanded meticulous attention to detail and prolonged periods of focused concentration. Now, he found himself having difficulty concentrating, his mind drifting during crucial meetings, or rereading the same paragraph in a policy brief multiple times without absorbing its content. Deadlines, once met with ease, now loomed as insurmountable obstacles, further eroding his self-confidence. Personally, Elijah had come to believe that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. The vibrant joy he once found in his grandchildren's laughter or the quiet satisfaction of a well-crafted argument had been replaced by a dull ache, a profound sense of loss that felt permanent. The emotional detachment during his memory recall seemed to confirm this appraisal; it was as if a part of him had died on that operating table.

The cumulative toll of these changes finally prompted Elijah to seek help. He was tired of the relentless tension, the unpredictable shifts between emotional numbness and overwhelming terror, and the gnawing fear that his body was a ticking time bomb. He longed for the peace he once knew, but his deepest fear was that this new, fearful existence was his permanent reality, a life sentence imposed by a body he no longer recognized as his own.
